title: Questions That Get a Real Answer
objective: Write four open questions for the employer encounter, using the approved employer card and topic list, and test every one against the yes-or-no check.

blocks.text: GROW · ASDAN · Week 6. ASDAN cross-strand. Questions That Get a Real Answer.
Objective: write four open questions for the employer encounter, using the approved employer card and topic list, and test every one against the yes-or-no check.
Success evidence: four questions on the project log, each with a topic named beside it, each checked and numbered in order.

Every question comes from the approved topic list and the employer card. You ask about the job. You are not asked about your home, your family or your beliefs, and you do not ask the visitor about theirs.
This log is your early project task for the class community project.
40 minutes. Offline.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Employer card and topic list on every desk before pupils sit down. Nobody writes a question before they have both.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil starts on their own home or family, point at the topic list and say we are asking about the job. Do not discuss it further.

blocks.text: An open question buys you an answer
Next week an employer visits our class community project.
You get about ten minutes with them. Your questions have to work first time.
A closed question can be answered with yes or no.
An open question makes the visitor explain something to you.
Open questions start with what, how or why.
Say the ten-minute limit out loud. The time pressure is what makes the open-question rule worth learning, so do not skip it.
You need three things on the desk. The employer card, the topic list and your project log.
The topic list tells you what this visitor has agreed to talk about.
If a question is not on a topic from that list, it does not get asked.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Read both example questions aloud yourself. Do not ask the group which one is better before the timings are shown.

blocks.text: Ten minutes, two kinds of question
Here are two questions asked at last term's visit.
The first was: do you like your job? The answer was yes.
That took four seconds and gave the class nothing to write down.
The second was: what does a normal Monday look like for you?
The visitor talked for two minutes and named six different tasks.
The same visitor and the same ten minutes gave a very different amount of evidence.
The second question was not cleverer, only harder to answer in one word.

items: 2 · pick a topic from the approved list.
3 · open with what, how or why.
4 · check that yes or no cannot finish it.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model one question fully and stop. Let the group build the second one rather than showing four.

blocks.text: Building one question from the card
I take the employer card for the site manager and read all three of its duties.
Now I pick one topic from the approved list. I pick training.
Next I choose my opening word. I choose how, because how asks for a process.
My question is: how did you learn to do this job?
Then I run the check. Could the visitor answer that with yes or no?
They could not, so it stays on the log.

boxes.head: CHECK
boxes.line1: can yes or no finish it?

blocks.caption: Every question on the log has been through all four steps
blocks.title: From employer card to checked question
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows running left to right, from reading the card to the yes-or-no check

blocks.text: Watch what I did not ask: nothing about the visitor's family or their pay.
The card and the list are the guard, and they tell me what this person came to talk about.
Model the check out loud, including the moment of doubt. Pupils copy the steps they see you do, not the ones you describe.
One more thing about the check. Say the yes answer in your head, and if it sounds like a real reply the question is still closed.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Cards sorted at every table before any hand goes up. Nobody speaks until all three piles are made: open, closed and no topic.

blocks.text: Sort them, then match them
Eight question cards are on your table. Read them all first.
Sort the eight cards into two groups: open and closed.
Then match every open card to one topic on the approved list.
Two of the open cards match no topic at all. Put those two in their own pile.
Hold up the card your table argued about most, and say which group you chose.
Put every card in a pile even if your table is unsure, because a guess you can see is worth more than a blank space.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Keep a closed card visible while you repair it. The repair only teaches if the original stays in sight.

blocks.text: Turning a closed question open
You do not throw a closed question away. You repair it.
Take this one: do you work weekends? That earns a yes and stops.
Change the opening word. Ask: what does a weekend shift involve?
The topic did not change, only the first word.

blocks.caption: One topic asked two ways, and only one of them fills the log
blocks.title: The same topic, opened and closed
blocks.alt: Two boxes side by side, the second drawn with a broken outline, each showing the reply the question gets

blocks.text: There is a second repair: add and why to the end.
Now ask: what does a weekend shift involve, and why is it different?
That question gets you a task list and a reason in one go.
Be careful with why on its own. Why can sound like a complaint.
Put why after a what, and it sounds like interest instead.

items: Say the question out loud once.
Answer it yourself in one word.
If that worked, change the opening word.
Ask it again and listen for a longer reply.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by table, not by choice. Two minutes each way, timed out loud.

blocks.text: Test a question on your partner
Work in twos. Read one of your questions to your partner.
Your partner answers it as briefly as they honestly can.
If one word finished it, change your opening word and ask them again.
Then swap over. You answer theirs in the same short way.
Do not be kind here. A one-word answer now saves a wasted question on the day.
Your partner answers as the worker on the card, not as themselves.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe the pupil's exact words. Do not open a closed question for them; write it as it stands and let the check catch it.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil asks something personal about the visitor, say that topic is not on the list and offer the nearest one that is.

blocks.text: Four questions, checked and ordered
Work on your own now. Write four questions on the project log.
Each one uses a topic from the approved list. Write that topic beside it.
Each one starts with what, how or why.
Run the yes-or-no check on all four and tick the box.
Use four different topics. Four questions about training is one question asked four times.
Then number them one to four, with your best question first.
Ten minutes may only fit two of them, so the order matters.

items: Supported · two questions from the topic list, both checked.
Standard · four questions on four topics, all checked and numbered in order.
Stretch · as Standard, and add the follow-up you would ask after question one.

blocks.text: A follow-up is the question you ask because of the answer you were given.
If you finish early, repair one closed card from the We Do pile.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult answers in one word if they can, then hands the log straight back for the fix.

blocks.text: Read your first question to an adult
Read question one to the adult at your table.
They answer it in a single word if they can.
If one word finished it, change your opening word now.
Then choose your job for the day. Ask this question yourself, hand it to a partner to ask, or take notes while others ask.
All three jobs count as contributing to the class community project.
Write your choice and today's date on the log before you leave.
Your log goes in the project folder, not in your bag, because it is your evidence of an early project task.
